stories.teaser: The sabra cactus’s secret: tiny leaves that work the day shift
stories.headline: Ben-Gurion University researchers discover how the prickly pear saves water yet grows fast after rain
stories.why: Short-lived tiny leaves on new pads supply about a fifth of their carbon; without them pads grew a third smaller. Published in the Journal of Experimental Botany.
texts:
Israel’s beloved sabra cactus has a secret: tiny leaves that work the day shift.

Ben-Gurion University researchers found that new prickly pear pads sprout cone-shaped leaves about 1 cm long, which drop off after about six weeks. While the pads take in CO2 only at night to save water, these little leaves do it in daylight, supplying about a fifth of the carbon a young pad needs.

#Israel #Science #Nature #Desert

“The prickly pear has two gears,” says Prof. Ilya Gelfand of Ben-Gurion University. “When water arrives, it shifts into a second, fast gear.”

When the team removed the tiny leaves on new pads, or sealed them with clear nail polish, the pads ended up about a third smaller and almost 40% lighter after three weeks. The study is in the Journal of Experimental Botany.

#Israel #Science #Nature #Desert

How does a desert cactus save water and still grow fast after rain?

Researchers at Ben-Gurion University’s Jacob Blaustein Institutes for Desert Research found the answer in tiny, short-lived leaves on the prickly pear’s new pads. The finding matters well beyond Israel: the plant is grown on about 26 million dunams around the world for fruit, fodder and fighting desertification.

#Israel #Science #Nature #Desert
stories.og_title: הסוד של הצבר: העלים הזעירים שמאפשרים לו לצמוח במהירות במדבר

stories.teaser: An Israeli climber gave up his summit to save a stranger
stories.headline: Israeli climber gives up his Himalayan summit dream to help save a sick Dutch climber
stories.why: Tzachi Miara stayed at 6,000 meters on Ama Dablam to keep a 25-year-old with altitude sickness stable until he was evacuated.
texts:
He trained for two years to climb Ama Dablam. Then he gave up the summit to save a stranger.

Israeli climber Tzachi Miara was at the 6,000-meter camp on the Nepal peak when a 25-year-old Dutch climber fell severely ill with altitude sickness. Miara stayed with two other climbers to keep him stable and get help. The next morning, a rescue team evacuated him to a hospital in Kathmandu.

#Israel #Kindness #Mountaineering #Nepal

“This is so much more important to me than any summit,” says Israeli climber Tzachi Miara.

On Ama Dablam in Nepal, 6,812 meters high, Miara stayed behind with Xenia Santha and Paul Clarke to help a Dutch climber who had lost consciousness. They found the man’s Sherpa guide and sent him for an oxygen tank from a lower camp, which saved the climber’s life.

#Israel #Kindness #Mountaineering #Nepal

Sometimes the bravest climb is the one you don’t finish.

Tzachi Miara had dreamed of Ama Dablam since he got into mountaineering in Nepal in 2019. Close to the top, he chose instead to care for a sick young Dutch climber until rescuers arrived. “I am glad we were in the right place at the right time,” he says. He plans to return next year.

#Israel #Kindness #Mountaineering #Nepal
stories.og_title: Israeli abandons Himalayan summit dream to help save sick climber

stories.teaser: Israeli medical tech reaching remote villages in Africa
stories.headline: ImpactWell brings Israeli medical technology to remote villages in Ghana, Malawi and Zambia
stories.why: Run by JDC with the Ruderman Family Foundation; JDC says more than 50,000 patients treated and 1,600 rural health workers trained since 2023.
texts:
In parts of rural Africa, reaching a doctor can mean the difference between life and death.

ImpactWell, an initiative of JDC with the Ruderman Family Foundation, brings Israeli medical technology to remote villages, from mobile X-rays to portable blood labs. Launched in Ghana in 2023, it has expanded to Malawi and Zambia. JDC says more than 50,000 patients have been treated and 1,600 rural health workers trained.

#Israel #SocialImpact #GlobalHealth #Africa

“This clinic brought me relief when I had nowhere else to turn,” says Esther Phiri of Chagwirira Village, Malawi.

Her clinic is part of ImpactWell, run by JDC with the Ruderman Family Foundation. In Ghana, a tuberculosis pilot using Israeli technology screened 4,500 patients and found about 2,000 with active TB or other lung diseases, according to JDC.

#Israel #SocialImpact #GlobalHealth #Africa

How do you bring modern medicine to villages far from any hospital?

ImpactWell, run by JDC with the Ruderman Family Foundation, pairs Israeli technologies (11 piloted so far) with local partners: nurses on bikes bringing prenatal and postnatal care, training in point-of-care ultrasound, and work alongside each country’s health ministry. The goal is for communities to provide better healthcare themselves.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #SocialImpact #GlobalHealth #Africa
stories.og_title: Bringing healthcare to the last mile: how Israeli innovation is changing lives in Africa and beyond

stories.teaser: A breast cancer risk check for 1.2 million women, from age 25
stories.headline: Clalit reaches out to 1.2 million Israeli women with an AI-based breast cancer risk check from age 25
stories.why: A nationwide, proactive questionnaire whose results go to each woman’s family doctor with personalized recommendations.
texts:
Israel’s largest health organization is reaching out to about 1.2 million women about their breast cancer risk, starting at age 25.

Clalit Health Services is inviting women aged 25–74 to fill in a digital questionnaire on personal, genetic and family history. An AI-based system assesses each woman’s risk, even without symptoms, and sends the results to her family doctor, with recommendations such as earlier mammograms or genetic testing.

#Israel #Health #BreastCancer #AI

“It allows us to look at each woman individually, rather than relying solely on general recommendations,” says Dr. Tatiana Dorfman of Clalit.

Routine screening usually starts at 50. Clalit’s new nationwide initiative uses a clinically validated questionnaire and its AI-PRO system to flag younger women who may need earlier screening, a breast surgeon consultation, or BRCA1/BRCA2 genetic testing.

#Israel #Health #BreastCancer #AI

A breast cancer risk check that comes to you, not the other way around.

Clalit Health Services is proactively contacting about 1.2 million women aged 25–74. Their answers go into their medical records, and family doctors receive personalized recommendations. “A recommendation to consult a breast surgeon does not necessarily indicate suspicion of disease,” says Dr. Lihi Eisen of Clalit.

#Israel #Health #BreastCancer #AI
stories.og_title: Israeli AI initiative targets breast cancer risk from age 25

stories.headline: Israeli researchers identify 15,000-year-old clay figurines, the earliest in Southwest Asia, some shaped by children
stories.why: A re-examination of 154 Natufian clay pieces from three sites in northern Israel pushes the tradition back by up to 3,000 years.
texts:
15,000 years ago, children in what is now Israel helped make some of the oldest clay figurines in the region, and left their fingerprints behind.

A Hebrew University–led team re-examined 154 Natufian clay pieces from Eynan-Mallaha, Hayonim Terrace and el-Wad Terrace. Fingerprints, tool marks and pigment show deliberate artwork: the earliest known clay figurines in Southwest Asia.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science

“What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects,” says Dr. Laurent Davin, who led the study.

One figurine carries two overlapping prints: a young or adult woman’s, and a child’s. Most of the 15 recognizable figurines depict birds, and one is coated with red engobe, the earliest known use of that technique.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science

Thousands of years before farming, people here were already sculpting clay.

A new study by Israeli and French researchers pushes the start of clay figurine-making in Southwest Asia back by as much as 3,000 years, to about 15,000 years ago. “These discoveries change how we understand the beginnings of artistic expression in this region,” says Dr. Laurent Davin.

#Israel #Archaeology #History #Science
stories.og_title: Israeli researchers find earliest clay figurines in Southwest Asia

stories.teaser: Volunteers rescue a rare black vulture in the Harod Valley
stories.headline: Volunteers and Israel’s wildlife hospital rescue a rare black vulture found weak in the Harod Valley
stories.why: Birdwatchers, a volunteer, rescuers and vets worked together; the vulture is gaining weight and recovering.
texts:
A rare black vulture was found weak by fish ponds in Israel’s Harod Valley. Volunteers made sure it got help.

After birdwatchers reported it, volunteer Tzukit Raviv found the bird. Yehonatan Ben Simon, a volunteer with the Nature and Parks Authority’s wildlife rescue unit, caught it and brought it to the Wildlife Hospital in Ramat Gan, where it is gaining weight and gradually recovering.

#Israel #Nature #Wildlife #Volunteering

“I was very moved. Her foot was the size of my hand,” says volunteer Yehonatan Ben Simon.

He caught a rare black vulture found weak near the Nir David fish ponds in the Harod Valley and took it to the Wildlife Hospital in Ramat Gan. Veterinarian Dr. Shira Gonen says the bird arrived in very poor condition, likely because an old fracture made it hard to find food.

#Israel #Nature #Wildlife #Volunteering

It took a whole chain of people to save one rare bird.

Birdwatchers spotted a weak black vulture in the Harod Valley. A volunteer found it, a Nature and Parks Authority bird ecologist advised, volunteer rescuers caught it, and the Wildlife Hospital in Ramat Gan is now treating it. The vulture is gaining weight and gradually recovering.

#Israel #Nature #Wildlife #Volunteering

stories.teaser: A Jerusalem squash club where Jewish and Arab kids train together
stories.headline: A new Jerusalem squash club brings Jewish and Arab children onto the same court
stories.why: 57 children, about half Jewish and half Arab, in its first months; 94% of kids who try a session stay, and school outreach has reached 723 children.
texts:
“It doesn’t matter here who is Jewish and who is Arab,” says Liel, 9.

Liel plays at a new squash club at the Jerusalem Tennis Center, where 57 children, about half Jewish and half Arab, train together. Founder Boaz Hirsch, 24, a former Israeli national team player, says 94% of the children who come for a trial session stay.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Sport #Jerusalem

A squash club in Jerusalem is bringing Jewish and Arab kids onto the same court.

Opened about two and a half months ago at the Jerusalem Tennis Center, together with the Jerusalem Municipality, the club already has 57 children. Its school outreach program has reached 723 children across the city. “Our ultimate goal is to create outstanding squash players,” says founder Boaz Hirsch.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Sport #Jerusalem

How do you bring kids from different communities together? Give them a racket.

At a new Jerusalem squash club, any child who wants to can play, “without distinction of race, religion or gender,” says Danny Mizrahi, who manages the Jerusalem Tennis Center. Coaches visit schools, invite kids to a trial session, and Jewish and Arab children then train side by side.

An idea any community could borrow.

#Israel #SocialImpact #Sport #Jerusalem
stories.og_title: "זה לא משנה כאן מי יהודי ומי ערבי": מועדון הסקווש שמחבר בין ילדי ירושלים

stories.teaser: An Israeli photographs the Space Station from the ground
stories.headline: An Israeli astronomer photographs the International Space Station from the ground in exceptional detail
stories.why: Michael Tsukran runs Tel Aviv University’s optical ground station; NASA astronaut Anil Menon shared his photo.
texts:
An Israeli photographed the International Space Station from the ground in exceptional detail.

Michael Tsukran, an astronomy lecturer who runs Tel Aviv University’s optical ground station, uses professional telescopes and precise tracking to catch the station, which moves at about 28,000 km/h some 400 km up. NASA astronaut Dr. Anil Menon shared his photo on X.

#Israel #Space #Astronomy #Photography

“Think about it for a moment: a structure the size of a football field,” says Israeli astronomer Michael Tsukran.

From the ground, he photographs that structure, the International Space Station, racing overhead at about 28,000 km/h, sometimes with only seconds to get the shot. His images even show the station before and after new solar panels were installed.

#Israel #Space #Astronomy #Photography

“You don’t have to be astronauts to explore the universe,” says Michael Tsukran.

After more than two decades of watching the sky, the Israeli astronomy lecturer, who runs Tel Aviv University’s optical ground station, photographs the Space Station, the Sun, planets and galaxies, and leads desert stargazing tours. “I want to show people that space is much closer than they think.”

#Israel #Space #Astronomy #Photography
